topics.title: Cache hits, misses and hit ratio

kcs.statement: A cache hit returns data from the cache without touching the backing store; a cache miss forces a read from the slower backing store.
Cache hit ratio = hits / (hits + misses), measured over a window of requests.
Average read latency ≈ hit ratio × cache latency + (1 − hit ratio) × (cache check + store latency), and raising the hit ratio from 90% to 99% cuts reads reaching the store tenfold.

serves.reason: Justifying a cache in the diagram needs the hit-ratio arithmetic that shows how much read load it removes from the database

topics.title: Where to cache: client, CDN, server, database, app

kcs.statement: Caches can sit at the client, the CDN, the web server or reverse proxy, the database and the application; the closer to the user, the more latency saved but the less control over invalidation.
Caching assembled objects keyed by id is easier to invalidate than caching database query results keyed by query text, because one changed row can affect many cached queries.

topics.title: Cache-aside: the default caching pattern

kcs.statement: With cache-aside, a read checks the cache; on a miss the application loads the value from the database and then writes it into the cache.
In cache-aside the application talks to both the cache and the database; the cache never reads from or writes to the database itself.
Cache-aside caches only data that is actually requested and survives a cache outage because reads fall back to the database, but each miss costs three trips and entries can go stale.

serves.reason: Cache-aside is the default strategy to name and justify for read-heavy workloads
Almost every classic mock prompt places a cache-aside layer in front of the database

requires.reason: The read path is defined by what happens on a hit versus a miss

topics.title: Cache invalidation and TTLs

kcs.statement: A TTL makes a cache entry expire a fixed time after it is written, so a cached value is never more than one TTL older than the write that produced it.
Explicit invalidation removes or updates the cache entry when the source data changes; keeping a TTL as well bounds staleness when an invalidation message is lost.
On a write it is safer to delete the cache key than to set the new value, because two concurrent writers can update the cache in the opposite order from the database and leave a stale value.

serves.reason: A justified cache strategy must state how entries are kept fresh and how stale a read can be

requires.reason: Invalidation is taught as the write half of the cache-aside pattern

topics.title: Read-through and write-through caching

kcs.statement: With read-through, the application reads only from the cache, and on a miss the cache itself loads the value from the database.

With write-through, each write goes through the cache, which synchronously persists it to the database before acknowledging; the cache matches the database only if every writer uses this path, writes to a key are applied in the same order to both, and a failed database write is not left in the cache.
Write-through adds write latency because each write touches both stores, and it fills the cache with data that may never be read, so it is often paired with a TTL.

serves.reason: Choosing between cache-aside and write-through is the core of justifying a cache against the read/write ratio

requires.reason: Read-through and write-through are defined by contrast with who loads the data in cache-aside

topics.title: Write-behind and write-around

kcs.statement: With write-behind (write-back), a write is acknowledged once it is in the cache and is flushed to the database asynchronously later, giving low write latency but losing unflushed writes if the cache fails.
With write-around, writes go directly to the database and bypass the cache, so the cache fills only on reads and recently written data misses on its first read.
Write-behind suits write-heavy data that tolerates some loss, such as view counters; write-around suits data written once and rarely re-read, such as logs.

requires.reason: Both are taught as variations on the write-through write path

topics.title: Refresh-ahead caching

kcs.statement: Refresh-ahead reloads a frequently read entry before its TTL expires, so readers do not pay miss latency, but it wastes database work when it refreshes entries nobody reads again.

topics.title: Choosing a cache strategy from the read/write ratio

kcs.statement: For a read-heavy workload (for example 100 reads per write) cache-aside or read-through with a TTL is the default; when a user must see their own write immediately, the design must add an explicit read-your-writes mechanism, such as routing every write through write-through or invalidating the key before acknowledging the write.
A complete cache choice names the pattern, the TTL and the staleness cost, and ties each to the stated read-to-write ratio and freshness requirement.

topics.title: Eviction policies and building an LRU cache

kcs.statement: An eviction policy decides which entry to remove when the cache is full; it is separate from TTL expiry, which removes entries by age.
LRU evicts the entry whose last access is oldest, and supports O(1) get and put using a hash map combined with a doubly linked list or an ordered map.
LFU evicts the least frequently accessed entry and keeps long-term popular items, while FIFO evicts the oldest inserted entry regardless of how often it is used.

requires.reason: Eviction is defined by contrast with TTL expiry

topics.title: Distributed and global caches

kcs.statement: A distributed cache spreads keys across several cache nodes, usually by hashing the key, so total cache memory and throughput grow with the number of nodes.
With hash(key) mod N placement, going from N to N+1 nodes moves about N/(N+1) of the keys to a different node, causing a burst of cache misses.
A per-server local cache is fastest but duplicates data and diverges across servers, while a shared global cache gives every stateless server the same view at the cost of a network hop.

serves.reason: Placing a cache tier for a large workload requires sizing and partitioning it across nodes

requires.reason: Local vs global builds on the application cache layer

topics.title: Hot keys and the thundering herd

kcs.statement: A hot key is a single key receiving a disproportionate share of traffic; because it lives on one cache node, adding nodes does not spread its load, so it is replicated or cached locally on each server.
A thundering herd (cache stampede) happens when a popular entry expires or is evicted and many concurrent misses all query the database at once to rebuild it.
Request coalescing (one rebuild per key while others wait), TTL jitter (randomised expiry times) and refresh-ahead each prevent stampedes on popular keys.

requires.reason: Hot keys are a problem of one key pinned to one cache node
Stampedes are triggered by TTL expiry
